passages.t: A sick child, a disguise, and a blind prophet who sees
passages.happening:
Jeroboam's son Abijah falls ill (verse 1). Jeroboam tells his wife to disguise herself and go to Shiloh, to Ahijah, the prophet who had told him he would be king, and to take him bread, cakes and a jar of honey (verses 2-3). Ahijah is old and blind, but the LORD tells him who is coming (verses 4-5). As soon as he hears her footsteps at the door, he says, “Come in, wife of Jeroboam! Why are you disguised? For I have been sent to you with bad news” (verse 6).

The message is for Jeroboam. God raised him up and tore the kingdom from David's house to give it to him, but he has not been like David. He has made other gods and images, and ‘you have flung Me behind your back’ (verse 9). So disaster will come on his house: every male cut off, and those who die left unburied (verses 10-11).

As for the boy: when her feet enter the city, he will die. ‘All Israel will mourn for him and bury him’ (verse 13), because he alone in Jeroboam's house will be buried with honor, ‘because only in him has the LORD, the God of Israel, found any good in the house of Jeroboam’ (verse 13). And one day the LORD will uproot Israel from the good land and scatter them beyond the Euphrates, because of the sins Jeroboam caused them to commit (verses 15-16).

She goes home to Tirzah, and as she crosses the threshold of the house, the boy dies. They bury him, and all Israel mourns him, ‘according to the word that the LORD had spoken through His servant Ahijah the prophet’ (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
The prophet who once gave Jeroboam ten pieces of a torn cloak (11:29-39) now takes back the gift, because Jeroboam refused its condition. Consulting a prophet about a sick child was normal, and a gift of food was the expected payment. Jeroboam sends his wife in disguise because he knows he has broken with the prophet who made him king and fears an unwelcome answer.

The scene is built on irony. A blind prophet sees through a disguise meant to fool him, and the woman who came to learn her son's future learns the future of her whole house. Ahijah's speech has the usual shape of a prophet's word of judgment: God's gifts, the sin, then the penalty.

To lie unburied, eaten by dogs and birds, was the worst fate an ancient person could imagine, cut off from family and honor. That is why it counts as mercy that this child will be mourned and buried.

Ahijah's words look far ahead, to the scattering of the north by Assyria two centuries later. Tirzah, in the hills northeast of Shechem, served as a royal residence and later as the northern capital until Omri moved it to Samaria.
passages.later: The scattering came in 722 BC: ‘the king of Assyria captured Samaria and carried away the Israelites to Assyria’ (2 Kings 17:6). And Isaiah says of the righteous who die young that ‘the righteous are guided from the presence of evil’ (Isaiah 57:1).
passages.hard:
Why does the one good child in Jeroboam's house die?

The text frames the boy's death as a strange mercy within judgment. Ahijah says that he alone will be buried and mourned by all Israel, because the LORD found something good in him. The rest of Jeroboam's house will die violently and lie unburied when Baasha seizes the throne (15:29). In the ancient view, a peaceful death and an honored burial were far better than what was coming.

Many readers still find this hard, and the chapter does not claim to answer every question about the suffering of the innocent. It does insist that God saw the child, valued him, and did not treat him as only a part of his father's guilt. Isaiah expresses a similar thought, that the righteous are sometimes taken away from evil to come.

Grief is not a lack of faith. If your grief is so heavy that you cannot carry it, please tell someone: a pastor, a friend, a doctor or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Jeroboam tried to hear God's word in disguise. Ask where you want God's help without wanting God to see you as you are. And ask what good God sees in someone you are inclined to write off with their family.

passages.t: Rehoboam's Judah, and bronze for gold
passages.happening:
Jeroboam's reign closes with the book's formula. His acts are written in ‘the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel’ (verse 19); he reigned twenty-two years, and his son Nadab reigned after him (verse 20).

The story turns south. Rehoboam was forty-one when he became king, and he reigned seventeen years in Jerusalem, ‘the city the LORD had chosen from all the tribes of Israel in which to put His Name’ (verse 21). His mother was Naamah the Ammonite. Judah does evil, more than their fathers had done. They build high places, sacred pillars and Asherah poles ‘on every high hill and under every green tree’ (verse 23), and there are male shrine prostitutes in the land (verse 24).

‘In the fifth year of Rehoboam’s reign, Shishak king of Egypt came up and attacked Jerusalem’ (verse 25). He takes the treasures of the temple and the palace, everything, ‘including all the gold shields that Solomon had made’ (verse 26). Rehoboam makes bronze shields in their place, and the guards carry them when the king goes to the house of the LORD (verses 27-28). There is war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam all their days. Rehoboam dies, and his son Abijam reigns in his place (verses 30-31).
passages.hearers:
From here Kings moves back and forth between the two kingdoms, reign by reign, and each account closes with a set formula. The Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel, and of Judah, were royal records the writer used and named. They are lost, and they are not the books of Chronicles in the Bible.

Judah, the kingdom that kept the temple, is no better than the north. The sacred pillars and Asherah poles were fixtures of Canaanite worship. Asherah was a goddess known from texts at Ugarit and elsewhere, and the Asherah was a wooden pole or stylized tree that stood for her. Inscriptions from about 800 BC and the eighth century, at Kuntillet Ajrud and Khirbet el-Qom, speak of the LORD and his asherah, which shows that some Israelites mixed her worship with the LORD's, exactly what the prophets condemned. The Hebrew word behind male shrine prostitutes means a consecrated person; whether it means ritual prostitution or other roles at the shrines is debated.

Shishak's campaign is one of the best-attested events of the period outside the Bible. Sheshonq I of Egypt recorded a campaign into Canaan on a relief at the temple of Amun at Karnak, listing many places, mostly in the Negev and the northern kingdom; a piece of a monument bearing his name was also found at Megiddo. Jerusalem does not clearly appear in what survives of the damaged list, which fits the Bible's account that the city paid rather than fell. Rehoboam's fifth year is usually dated about 926 or 925 BC.

The bronze shields measure how far Solomon's splendor had fallen in five years. Rehoboam's mother is twice called an Ammonite (verses 21, 31), a reminder of Solomon's marriages in chapter 11.
passages.later: Chronicles adds that the prophet Shemaiah came to Rehoboam when Shishak attacked, and that the king and the leaders humbled themselves and said, “The LORD is righteous” (2 Chronicles 12:6).
passages.asks: Rehoboam kept up the ceremony with bronze where there had been gold. Ask where you are keeping up appearances after the real thing has been lost. And ask whether the faith of the place you belong to is any purer than that of the people you look down on.
